title: Hotel Key Card Sample Planning Guide
summary: A sample-planning guide for hotels that ties the first sample round back to lock compatibility, encoder fleet, material shortlist, encoding scope, artwork readiness and rollout timing — so the first 200 cards answer one decision instead of raising a dozen new ones.
heroPoints: The best sample round answers one decision at a time — not every possible card variant in a single shipment.
A control sample that matches the lock firmware always ships first, even if the property expects to order a premium material.
A sharper brief saves more time than a larger assortment — six variants delay decisions, two variants accelerate them.
imageAlt: Hotel sample planning session with control and premium card options

sections.title: Why sample planning is the real hotel procurement leverage
sections.intro: Most procurement teams treat sampling as a logistics detail — ask, receive, approve. That's why sample cycles slip. Sample planning is the single highest-leverage step in the whole hotel card project.
bullets: Every open question the sample round does not resolve becomes a question the pilot has to resolve — and the pilot costs ten times as much to re-run.
The sample brief is the only moment in the project when the supplier and the property share exactly the same information. Once production starts, divergence grows fast.
A well-scoped sample round converts ambiguous brand direction into a concrete pass/fail test. Without that conversion, the project drifts on vibes.

sections.title: The control sample comes first, always
sections.intro: The control sample is the known-good card that matches the lock firmware. It is the baseline that every upgraded material has to beat to earn a place in the final order.
bullets: Chip family and encoding: must match the lock and encoder estate. Retrofits usually land on MIFARE Classic 1K or DESFire EV3; greenfield properties standardise on DESFire EV3.
Substrate and thickness: CR80 in standard PVC or recycled PVC at 0.76–0.84 mm. This is the thickness the lock firmware has been tested against for years.
Print: a minimum viable design that carries the property name, room identifier (if used) and legal text. Not the final artwork.
Purpose: validate lock opening, encoder handling, issue speed, replacement flow and durability under staff handling. Nothing more.
Exit criterion: the control sample has to pass the lock pilot before any upgraded material earns a conversation. Properties that skip this step spend the first order on rework.

sections.title: The upgraded sample: one option, not three
sections.intro: The upgraded sample reflects the brand ambition. The discipline is to pick one — not to sample every material on the supplier catalogue.
bullets: Brand-first shortlist: wood, recycled PVC with high post-consumer content, PLA, rPET, bio-composite. One of these, based on the property positioning decided before the sample round starts.

Compatibility rider: require the supplier to tune the chip antenna for the upgraded substrate and confirm lock compatibility on the real lock firmware. Wood and PLA are not automatic on PVC-tuned antennas.
Print method match: the upgraded substrate constrains the print method. UV for wood, dye-sub for PLA, offset for recycled PVC. Confirm the print method upfront, not after the proof arrives.
Durability sample: request at least 20 upgraded cards for a two-week staff-handling round. Visual wear shows up fast.
Decision rule: write down before the samples arrive what result would swing the decision from control to upgraded. Without that rule, decisions drift for weeks.

sections.title: Scope the brief so the supplier replies once, not three times
sections.intro: RFQ cycles stretch when the supplier has to ask a follow-up question. A complete brief packaged as one PDF eliminates most of those follow-ups.
bullets: Property profile: number of rooms, lock firmware list, encoder fleet, PMS and middleware, chain affiliation if any, expected annual card volume, replacement-rate estimate.
Chip family and encoding scope: preferred chip, fallback chip, pre-encoding scope (blank, partial, full), key-handling method, any chain-level security standard.
Material shortlist: one control and one upgraded alternative. Name them explicitly. Do not ask the supplier to propose materials from scratch.
Numbering and print rules: whether cards carry unique printed serials, room-range numbering, loyalty variants, language variants.
Sample quantities and timing: the control quantity (typically 200 for the lock pilot), the upgraded quantity (typically 50 for brand review), delivery address, target arrival date.
Decision timeline: when the property decides on the control, when on the upgraded, when the full order is placed.
Compliance and certification: any required certifications on the upgraded sample (GRS, FSC, TÜV OK Compost). Ask for the certificate number upfront.
Exit criteria: what has to pass for each sample to earn a production order. Written, not verbal.

sections.title: Pilot sizing and placement
sections.intro: The pilot quantity should be informed by the property size, the issue rate, and the confidence the sample has to build.
bullets: Small property (<100 rooms): 100 control cards plus 30 upgraded cards is usually enough for a two-week pilot.
Mid property (100–300 rooms): 200 control cards plus 50 upgraded cards. Covers peak check-in throughput testing.
Large property (>300 rooms): 400 control cards plus 100 upgraded cards. Pilot has to cover multiple front desks, lift overrides and staff master card workflows.

Multi-property chain: one pilot property runs the full stack; other properties receive reference samples only. Chain rollouts should not parallel-pilot ten properties — the variance swamps the signal.

Geographic placement: if the chain has properties in different climates, pilot at the most extreme (coastal humidity or desert heat) first. Easier climates rarely surprise after a hard-climate pilot passes.

sections.title: Running the sample round without burning weeks
sections.intro: Once the samples arrive, the workflow decides whether the decision lands in days or months.
bullets: Day 0: unbox, inventory, confirm numbering matches the delivery note, inspect for shipping damage.
Day 1: compatibility round — issue 50 control cards through the real PMS, test opening across every lock firmware, measure issue speed at peak check-in.
Day 2–3: replacement workflow — lose cards on purpose, re-issue, confirm invalidation latency; test housekeeping override, master cards, DND.
Day 4–10: durability round — 20 cards rotated through staff handling, guest simulation, pocket wear, pool-bag moisture.
Day 11–13: brand review — upgraded samples evaluated against the positioning brief, proof reviewed by brand and operations together.
Day 14: decision meeting — does the control pass? Does the upgraded earn the slot? If either answer is no, document what needs to change and decide whether to re-sample or adjust scope.
Week 3–4: production order placed if both samples passed. Sample round that drifts past week four almost always signals an unresolved upstream issue (compatibility, positioning, or budget).

sections.title: Common sample-round failure patterns
sections.intro: The same failure modes recur across properties. Recognising them early saves weeks.
bullets: Over-ordering variants: six materials arrive, the team cannot decide, the round adds two weeks. Fix: always narrow to control + one upgraded before samples ship.
Skipping the control: the property samples wood first to save a step, lock compatibility fails on the substrate, the project restarts. Fix: control always ships.
Pilot scope creep: the operations team adds lobby self-check-in kiosks to the pilot midway through. Fix: freeze pilot scope before samples arrive.
Ambiguous decision rules: 'see how it feels' replaces written exit criteria. Fix: write the pass/fail conditions before unboxing.
Late brand review: brand team sees the proof for the first time at week four. Fix: brief brand in at sample scoping, not sample review.
No re-sample budget: everyone assumes the first sample round will land clean. Fix: reserve two weeks and 20% of sample cost for a second round that might not be needed.

faq.question: How many hotel key card samples should a first round include?
faq.answer: Two sample types: one control card that matches the lock firmware and a baseline PVC substrate, and one upgraded alternative that reflects the brand ambition. Quantities vary by property size — 100–400 control cards and 30–100 upgraded cards — but the variant count stays at two. More than that slows the decision without producing a clearer outcome.

faq.question: What speeds up a hotel sample request most?
faq.answer: A complete one-page brief that covers lock firmware, encoder fleet, PMS, chip family, encoding scope, substrate shortlist, numbering rules, pilot quantity, delivery timing and written exit criteria. Suppliers reply in two weeks when this document is complete; they reply in six weeks when the brief only covers finish preference and arrival date.

faq.question: Can a hotel skip the control sample if the team already trusts the material?
faq.answer: No. The control sample is what proves the chip, encoding and lock firmware match before the upgraded material changes substrate behaviour. Properties that skip the control spend their first production order on rework when the upgraded card passes a reference reader but fails the real lock.

faq.question: Who has to sign off on the sample round?
faq.answer: Three stakeholder groups — brand, operations and compliance — exactly as with artwork. Brand signs the upgraded sample; operations signs the control; compliance signs any certification or sustainability claim on the upgraded sample. Documenting all three sign-offs before placing the production order prevents cross-team surprises in week five.

faq.question: How should a multi-property chain run sample planning?
faq.answer: One lead property runs the full sample round and pilot. Other properties receive reference samples only, plus a compatibility rider for any material that differs from the lead. Parallel pilots across ten properties produce so much variance that no clean decision can be made; a single anchor pilot followed by rolling replication is faster and more reliable.

faq.question: What is the correct response when the sample round is ambiguous?
faq.answer: Adjust scope, do not re-order more samples. Ambiguity almost always signals an upstream issue — unclear positioning, unclear chip family, or unclear exit criteria. Ordering more variants compounds the ambiguity. The right move is to document what is unclear, resolve it, then re-sample a focused round.

faq.question: What is the single biggest avoidable mistake in hotel sample planning?
faq.answer: Letting the brand team treat sampling as a design exercise when the first question is still technical fit. Technical validation has to pass on the control card before material upgrades matter. Inverting that order is the most common reason hotel card projects burn their first order on rework.
